title: NPV
explanation: Should a café spend $50,000 on a new espresso bar that brings in cash over 5 years? Adding up the cash isn't enough, because money later is worth less than money now. **NPV** (net present value) converts every future cash flow into today's dollars and adds them up. If NPV is positive, the project creates value.

tasks.prompt: In B6, try the obvious formula: =NPV(B2, B4:G4). This is a classic mistake, so watch the result.
tasks.teach: **NPV(rate, cash flows)** assumes the **first** cash flow happens **one year from now**. But the $50,000 is spent **today** (year 0), so this formula wrongly discounts it as if it were paid a year later.
hints: It's the wrong answer on purpose.

tasks.prompt: In B7, do it the right way: NPV of years 1 to 5 only, then add the year-0 cash flow: =NPV(B2, C4:G4) + B4.
tasks.teach: Year-0 money is already in today's dollars, so it's added **outside** NPV. This is one of the most common finance interview questions.

tasks.prompt: Last one: in B8, show "Invest" if the right NPV is above 0, otherwise "Pass".

recap: NPV turns future cash flows into today's dollars. NPV assumes the first cash flow is a year away, so add the year-0 investment outside: =NPV(rate, years 1 to n) + year 0. Positive NPV means invest.
